reference_id: AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures
reference_title: AASHTO Guide for Design of Pavement Structures, 1993 Edition
chapter_title: Part I, Chapter 3 -- Economic Evaluation of Alternative Pavement Design Strategies

sections.title: Life-Cycle Cost Concepts and Economic Analysis Basics
sections.summary: Recommends life-cycle economic evaluation (present worth and/or equivalent uniform annual cost) over an analysis period to compare alternative pavement design/rehabilitation strategies, but cautions that pavement-type selection should not rest on economics alone (Appendix B provides broader selection guidelines).
sections.body: Chapter 3 (condensed here; printed guide Sections 3.1-3.8, pdf_page ~41-73, printed I-41 to I-49) covers life-cycle cost concepts (initial capital costs, maintenance, rehabilitation/resurfacing cost, salvage/residual value, user costs including traffic delay cost, and the identification of pavement benefit) and the discounting/inflation considerations (opportunity cost of capital, discount rates) needed for an economic evaluation. It stresses that economics should be A factor, not the SOLE factor, in pavement type selection; Appendix B provides an extensive list of guidelines for comparing alternative design strategies.
key_points: Life-cycle costs: initial capital, maintenance, rehabilitation/resurfacing, salvage/residual value, user costs
User costs include vehicle operating cost, travel time cost, accident cost, discomfort cost, and traffic delay cost
Discounting/inflation: opportunity cost of capital, discount rate selection
Economics should inform, not solely determine, pavement type selection (Appendix B: broader selection guidelines)
sections.applicability: Framing for comparing alternative design/rehabilitation strategies on a life-cycle cost basis.

sections.title: Equations for Economic Analysis
sections.summary: Two standard methods are given: Equivalent Uniform Annual Cost (EUAC) and Present Worth (net present value, NPV). NPV is generally preferred for pavements: NPVx1 = TPWCxo,n - TPWCx1,n (present worth of the base/standard alternative minus present worth of the alternative being evaluated); comparisons must use equal-length analysis periods regardless of method.
sections.body: Two methods for economic evaluation are presented (Section 3.9): the Equivalent Uniform Annual Cost method (Section 3.9.1) and the Present Worth (net present value) method (Section 3.9.2), NPVx1 = TPWCxo,n - TPWCx1,n, where TPWC is total present worth of costs for an alternative over an n-year analysis period, and xo is the standard/base alternative against which x1 is compared. The present worth (net present value) method is generally preferred for the highway field over the 'traditional' annual-cost and benefit-cost methods, offering several advantages: costs/benefits expressed as a single comparable value; direct comparability of projects with different service lives and stage development; all costs in present-day terms; ability to fold in nonmonetary (cost-effectiveness) considerations; a single payoff figure; and computational simplicity. Its chief disadvantage is that it cannot be applied to single (non-comparative) alternatives, and the lump-sum result may be less intuitively understandable as a rate of return. Most agencies use only the agency-cost term (Eq. 3.9.3, without the user-cost term) due to data/policy limitations. Section 3.9.3 concludes that either NPV or EUAC may be used for life-cycle comparisons, provided comparisons are made over analysis periods of EQUAL length.
key_points: NPVx1 = TPWCxo,n - TPWCx1,n (Eq. 3.9.7) -- present worth method, preferred for highways
TPWC = total present worth of costs for an alternative over an n-year analysis period
NPV advantages: single comparable value, handles differing service lives/staging, present-day terms, cost-effectiveness-compatible, computationally simple
NPV disadvantage: cannot evaluate a single non-comparative alternative; lump-sum less intuitive than a rate
Most agencies use agency-cost-only comparisons (Eq. 3.9.3), omitting the user-cost term
Either NPV or EUAC acceptable, but ONLY for analysis periods of equal length

equations.description: NPVx1 = TPWCxo,n - TPWCx1,n (net present value comparison)

sections.applicability: Comparing life-cycle costs of alternative pavement design or rehabilitation strategies over equal-length analysis periods.
